Thermal predictions start with an allocated article.

A usable study supplies the temperatures, properties and boundary conditions needed to calculate a result. This register explains those defaults, their sources and the specific hardware boundary each one represents.

The Quantum-2 MQM9700-NS2F reference uses forward airflow. Its published operating ambient interval informs a project allocation at the adapted network article. Allocation

The project’s proposed requirement at an identified body, sensor or interface. A reasoned engineering judgment can complete this baseline before supplier evidence exists.

Prediction

The calculated response to the selected properties, loads and environment. It can reveal missed targets, inadequate heat paths or an unstable dwell.

Verification evidence

Configuration-specific observations and reviewed results. An allocated range or completed numerical run does not establish a supplier rating or close a requirement.

Article temperature envelopes

These values are the implemented preliminary project requirements. Rows with manufacturer references explain the boundary conversion or reserve being assumed. Rows marked engineering judgment are project choices; NASA and ECSS do not supply one universal temperature interval for every part. The part’s Requirements panel retains its exact allocation, source and measurement boundary. GEVS — thermal-vacuum verification · ECSS-E-ST-31C — Thermal control

The non-operating interval is an allocated exposure-and-recovery requirement. Its name does not assert that recovery has been demonstrated. A material detail receives a declared local specimen or interface requirement; the parent’s qualification is not inherited.

Architecture-owned boundaries stay with the design

The existing accelerator, cold-plate, transport, radiator, battery and blanket requirements remain controlled design inputs. They take precedence over a generic component family. Relevant cold-plate, radiator, transport and blanket details receive explicit environmental requirement flowdown at their own declared specimen boundary.

Subsystems without an existing coupled vehicle node retain one local article temperature per directly allocated member. Different sensor, radio or propulsion items do not acquire a single shared allowable temperature simply because they belong to one subsystem.

Mass, materials and heat paths

Complete flight assemblies use their active master equipment list mass, quantity, geometry and dissipated power. Thermal storage is mass multiplied by the selected specific heat. Radiator area, finish, battery properties and architecture transport capacities use their corresponding design inputs. Detail estimates remain inside the parent mass allocation and never add a duplicate flight-ledger mass.

Constant heat capacities below are useful near-ambient model approximations. They do not implement temperature-dependent properties over the entire allocated envelope. Glass, composite, electronics and coating constructions need characterization; phase change, internal hot spots and contact nonlinearities are outside this reduction.

Details and representative coupons

A registered mechanical detail uses an explicit share of its parent article’s mass and exposed area, documented in the model field’s basis. Surface layers and details without a defensible separate envelope use a declared 100 × 100 mm specimen. The full-size rendering supplies context; the model’s scope identifies the coupon.

The model scope identifies each coupon’s thickness. Mass follows its planform area × thickness × the registered effective density; exposed area comprises the two specimen faces. A plated contact uses a copper substrate with a thin finish, not solid gold. Passive details have zero independent electrical dissipation; the powered parent case supplies the integrated load.

Mounting and the finite fixture

The contact estimate starts with 250 W/(m²·K), a nominal metal-contact example in the NASA thermal guide, multiplied by an allocated contact area of 2% of exposed area with a 2 cm² minimum. Actual finish, preload, contact geometry, interface materials and pressure can change that value substantially. A parallel design requirement sizes the mounting path for no more than a 5 K rise at the allocated heat load; it is a proposed heat path, not a measured joint. NASA Passive Thermal Control Engineering Guidebook v5.1

Gmount = max(0.05 W/K, 250 W/(m²·K) × Acontact, Qload / 5 K)
Carticle = mass × specific heat
Cfixture = clamp(0.1 × article mass, 0.05, 100) kg × 900 J/(kg·K)
Gconditioning = max(1 W/K, 5 × Gmount)

Battery and compute mounts use their existing design conductances. A contained liquid or gas exchanges heat with its vessel interface; its direct chamber radiation area is zero. The atmospheric scenario uses an explicit 5 W/(m²·K) air coefficient. Vacuum removes air convection. Infrared emittance and solar absorptance are physical input estimates independent of rendered color and texture.

The article target is not the chamber command

A powered article is generally warmer than its cooled mounting boundary. Setting both to the same number can miss the article criterion even after a long wait. The local test setup therefore derives an initial boundary command from the planned heat load, two conductances in series and radiation; an atmospheric case also includes convection.

Gseries = (1/Gmount + 1/Gconditioning)−1
Qload = Gseries(Tarticle − Tboundary)
  + εσA(Tarticle4 − Tshroud4)
  + hA(Tarticle − Tair) [atmosphere only]

The planned heat includes article dissipation and the enabled heater state at the target. The transient still resolves thermostat hysteresis. This is an initial engineering setup calculation, not a curve fitted to the desired transient result. The full time-dependent prediction still determines whether the article enters its target tolerance, stabilizes and completes uninterrupted dwell. If the requested setup fails, the result retains that failure. Explicit user boundary commands remain available.

The development baseline uses two cycles, a 30-minute dwell after stabilization, a 1 K/hour stabilization threshold observed over 5 minutes, ±2 K article target tolerance, and a 4-hour maximum plateau. The boundary ramp is no faster than the item rate allocation: typically 1 K/min, 0.5 K/min for optical or battery cases, and 0.25 K/min for the HPE-derived host. Vacuum pressure is 0.001 Pa. These are development-study choices, not an adopted qualification procedure.

Zero additional test margin is an intentional development default. Selecting qualification, protoflight or acceptance does not authorize that physical exposure or supply its tailored margin, life-consumption policy, functional checks or article disposition. Those remain distinct reviewed test-plan decisions. GSFC-STD-7000B — GEVS · GEVS — thermal-vacuum verification · NASA Passive Thermal Control Engineering Guidebook v5.1 · ECSS-E-ST-31C — Thermal control

Complete inputs, open engineering evidence

Planning budgets default to 1 K combined temperature measurement uncertainty, a 3 K model-correlation RMS error and a 2 K absolute signed bias. Article-gradient allocations vary with function: precision optical interfaces receive 2 K, attitude sensors and battery stores 5 K, many electronic articles 10 K, and structural or mechanism articles 20 K. Solar blankets use 30 K across their monitored article locations. These are explicit project criteria, not achieved measurements or universal standard limits.

A one-node article model cannot establish an internal gradient. Likewise, a numerical temperature cycle does not measure network throughput, drive torque, optical alignment, leak rate or battery recovery. Those observations belong to the linked functional and verification records. Calibration, correlation, selected supplier capability and authorized acceptance remain traceable tasks. NASA Systems Engineering Handbook — Product Verification · NASA Systems Engineering Handbook — Technical Planning

Publication readiness

The checks enumerate the catalog and the settings actually offered for each reference. Every offered thermal setting must resolve to a plan, allocated article targets, finite physical inputs, valid case steps and executable solver setup, with source IDs that resolve in the program. The broader engineering checks also inspect numerical inputs and outputs in other subsystem analyses. Deliberately deleting an allocation in a test must make the gate fail.

Changing an allocation, design reference or model revision changes the configuration identity. Earlier runs keep their original inputs, requirement revisions, article targets and plan snapshot. A failed target or an incomplete intentional user edit remains visible; publication readiness supplies complete defaults without weakening that validation.
